issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette:
Ramesh, a 58-year-old fisherman, had built his life around the rhythm of the ocean, a rhythm that shattered six months ago in a violent collision at sea. His small vessel, the *Sita*, was struck by a much larger commercial ship that vanished into the fog as quickly as it appeared, leaving Ramesh trapped amidst splintered wood and rising water. He had been certain he would die, watching his livelihood disintegrate around him, until strangers in a Coast Guard cutter pulled him from the wreckage, disoriented and badly injured. The lingering terror of that day had seeped into every corner of his existence.

Now, any "crash imagery," even just seeing cars hit by accident on a distant television screen, would instantly trigger a sickening plunge back into the chaotic moments of the collision. The memory would overwhelm him, feeling "like it is happening right now rather than something that is over," bringing back the same "terror he felt at the time." This persistent, vivid reliving of the event made him acutely aware of, and sensitive to, anything that might even vaguely resemble the accident, thus creating new triggers and intensifying existing ones. What was particularly distressing was that he knew what had happened, the sequence of events, but he was often "unable to find words to describe it" when pressed. This inability to articulate his experience made the memory feel even more isolated and potent, and the sheer "terror on recall" made him acutely sensitive to anything that remotely resembled the accident, so that any "crash imagery" became unbearable, making him avoid news and movies.

His internal world had become a landscape of suspicion. The accident had cemented a profound belief that "people are not what they seem," a conviction that extended to his own capabilities. He felt "he no longer knew himself anymore," and perhaps most unsettlingly, "he could no longer trust his own body" to keep him safe. These deeply held "negative appraisals" about himself and others fed a constant, gnawing sense of vulnerability. This profound belief that he was no longer capable or trustworthy in his own skin made the memory of the collision feel inescapable, as if the event itself was proof of his new, diminished reality. Because "he could no longer trust his own body" after the accident, he found himself constantly "on guard even inside his own home," interpreting "unusual silence" as a sign that "something dangerous is about to happen." This pervasive feeling of "threat in silence" and being perpetually "alert at home" reinforced his belief that "he didn't know himself anymore" and that his "body was unreliable," incapable of keeping him safe.

The constant state of "scanning his surroundings for signs of danger" made the memory of the accident more intrusive, causing it to "feel present not past," especially when he was alone on the dock or at home. This feeling of being "on guard" also made him acutely sensitive to even subtle cues, so that "unusual silence" in his usually bustling fishing community would make him flinch, interpreting it as a precursor to danger and causing him to react with profound suspicion to "stranger interaction." When "talking to strangers" became necessary—perhaps during resupply or at the fish market—Ramesh’s conviction that "people are not what they seem" was solidified, further reinforcing his general "distrust of others." The memory itself, feeling "like it is happening right now," constantly reinforced his belief that "he could no longer trust his own body" to protect him, and that "people are not what they seem," recalling the large ship that had simply vanished. His pervasive feeling of "threat in silence" and being "alert at home" further reinforced his belief that "he didn't know himself anymore" and that his "body was unreliable," unable to keep him safe.

The cumulative effect of these interwoven fears and memories had eroded his life. He found it increasingly difficult to work, the open water now a source of dread rather than solace. The thought of losing another loved one, a pain he knew well after his wife's passing, was amplified by his recent trauma. Any "talk about people losing loved ones" would send a cold shiver through him, reminding him of his own brush with death and the fragility of life. This constant fear of loss, coupled with his deep "distrust of others," had isolated him from his fishing community, leaving him feeling adrift. He had finally sought help, hoping to find a way to reclaim the man he once was, the man who knew the sea and trusted its currents, before the waves of terror consumed him entirely.
